title: Moving file uploads
question: Should we move customer file uploads to a new storage provider, change how uploads reach storage, or both?
summary: A mid-size web team stores customers' files with one storage provider. Large uploads time out, and the transfer bill keeps growing. This map shows how an upload works today, what each option changes, and what the team still has to decide. All figures are made up.
reading: The first view, How an upload works, has six journeys: an upload today, the proposed direct upload, downloading and sharing, deleting, moving existing files, and what happens when something goes wrong. Each column is a part of the system, from the customer's browser on the left to the storage provider on the right, so you can see where each step happens. The second view, Options, starts from the outcome we want and branches into problems, ideas and quick tests. Turn on Show technical names in any box to see the services and settings involved. Notes from security, finance, support and others sit on the steps they are about.

checked.note: Checked against the incident review, April upload numbers, 31 support tickets, a provider comparison and call notes, the scanning and retention setup, and a team discussion.

glossary.signed link: A web address that lets one browser upload or download one file for a few minutes, without a password.
glossary.proxy: When our servers pass every byte between the customer and storage, instead of the customer talking to storage directly.
glossary.resumable upload: An upload sent in pieces, so a dropped connection only loses the last piece.
glossary.data out: Files sent from storage to anyone outside it. Providers charge for this.
glossary.CDN: A network of servers close to customers that keeps copies of popular files, so they download faster and cost less.
glossary.checksum: A short fingerprint of a file. If two copies have the same checksum, they are the same.
glossary.holding area: A place where new files wait, unseen by anyone else, until the virus scan passes.
glossary.recycle area: Where a provider keeps deleted files for a few days in case they were deleted by mistake.

sources.title: Provider B call notes and draft terms

evidence.text: Uploads over 200 MB timed out for about 40 minutes.
Half our servers were just shovelling bytes. Nothing else could get through.
Our storage bill grew 22% last quarter, mostly from data transfer out, not storage.
Support received 31 tickets. Most from customers uploading video.
Data out: $90 per TB today; $0 to our CDN with provider B.
Moving 180 TB at current transfer prices would cost about $16,000 once. Provider B offers free one-time transfer over 100 TB, on request.
The real problem is the proxy, not the provider. Direct uploads fix the timeouts wherever the files live.
Customers ask for a progress bar and the ability to resume after a dropped connection.
Signed links must expire in minutes and only allow one file path.
Nobody has tested how virus scanning works if files no longer pass through our servers.
19 of 31 tickets were video uploads over 200 MB; 8 said it got to 90% and then failed.
I lost two hours re-uploading the same file three times.
Just show me how far along it is. I can't tell if it's stuck.
Our firewall blocks some sites. Will the new way still work here?
3.1% of uploads were over 200 MB, but they were 71% of all bytes uploaded.
Failure rate for uploads over 200 MB: 6.2% in busy hours, 1.4% at night.
Upload servers spend about 55% of their time passing bytes to storage.
18% of files are downloaded more than 10 times and make up 80% of data out.
Free one-time transfer needs a written request and approval, usually 2 to 3 weeks.
Provider B keeps deleted files 7 days in a recycle area unless turned off.
Upload completion messages go to a web address we choose; they retry for 24 hours.
Their EU region is in a different country from our current one. Legal must check our customer contracts.
Files are shown to the customer before the scan finishes; downloads are blocked only if the scan fails.
Scanning takes about 9 seconds under 100 MB and up to 4 minutes for 5 GB.
Our terms promise deleted files are gone within 30 days, including backups.
Bucket names at provider B are global; ours must be renamed.
Their onboarding team suggests writing new files to both providers for at least a month and comparing checksums on every file before switching reads.
Finance wants the transfer bill down before the September budget review.

maps.title: How an upload works
maps.intro: Six journeys from the customer's browser to the storage provider. Each column is the part of the system that does that step.

journeys.title: Upload today
journeys.summary: Every byte passes through our servers on its way to storage.

steps.text: Customer picks a file and presses Upload
steps.detail: Upload button on the files page; no size limit shown.

steps.text: Browser sends the whole file to our servers
steps.detail: One HTTP request per file, no pieces.
steps.pain: No progress bar; people cannot tell if it is stuck.

steps.text: Our servers pass the bytes on to storage
steps.detail: Streaming proxy in the upload service; 60-second idle timeout at the load balancer.

steps.text: Long uploads hold a server connection open
steps.detail: Each upload ties up one worker for its whole length.
steps.pain: Other customers' requests queue behind them.

steps.text: On weak wifi the upload fails and starts again from zero
steps.detail: No resume; the browser retries the whole request.

steps.text: File record is saved and the file shown to the customer
steps.detail: Row in the files table with size, type and owner.

steps.text: A job scans the file for viruses
steps.detail: Scanner reads the file from storage after the upload finishes.

steps.text: If the scan fails, downloads are blocked
steps.detail: Until then the file can already be shared and downloaded.
steps.pain: A bad file can be downloaded for up to 4 minutes.

journeys.title: Upload with direct links (proposed)
journeys.summary: The browser sends the file straight to storage in pieces, using a short-lived signed link.
creates: The file in a holding area

steps.text: Customer picks a file and presses Upload
steps.detail: Same button; size limit shown up front.

steps.text: Our servers check the customer may upload, and issue a signed link for one file
steps.detail: Signed link valid 10 minutes, one path, one content type.

steps.text: A file record is created in 'uploading' state
steps.detail: Status column: uploading, scanning, ready, rejected.

steps.text: Browser uploads straight to storage in pieces, with a progress bar
steps.detail: Multipart upload, 16 MB pieces, three in parallel.

steps.text: If the connection drops, the upload resumes from the last piece
steps.detail: Browser keeps the upload id and finished pieces in local storage.

steps.text: Some office firewalls may block the storage address
steps.detail: Fallback: the old proxy path for customers who cannot reach storage directly.
steps.pain: Schools and offices with strict firewalls.

steps.text: File lands in a holding area nobody else can read
steps.detail: Separate bucket prefix with no public or shared access.

steps.text: Storage tells us the upload finished; a job scans it
steps.detail: Completion message to our web address, retried for 24 hours.

steps.text: File is marked ready only after a clean scan
steps.detail: Moved out of the holding area, status set to ready.

steps.text: Customer sees 'Ready' or a plain message if it was rejected
steps.detail: Rejected files are deleted after 7 days; owner gets an email.

journeys.title: Downloading and sharing
journeys.summary: A customer or someone they share with downloads a file.

steps.text: Customer clicks Download, or opens a share link
steps.detail: Share links never expire unless the owner turns them off.

steps.text: Our servers check they may see the file
steps.detail: Owner, team member, or holder of a share link.

steps.text: Our servers make a signed download link
steps.detail: Valid 5 minutes, one file.

steps.text: Storage sends the file to the browser
steps.detail: Every download is billed as data out at $90 per TB.
steps.pain: This is where the bill grows.

steps.text: Popular files could come from the CDN instead
steps.detail: 18% of files make 80% of data out; caching them at the CDN cuts the bill.

steps.text: We count the download
steps.detail: Download counter on the file record.

steps.text: A file still being scanned cannot be downloaded
steps.detail: Today it can; in the planned flow it waits.

journeys.title: Deleting a file
journeys.summary: A customer deletes a file, or closes their account.

steps.text: Customer deletes a file
steps.detail: Moves to the customer's trash for 30 days.

steps.text: File is marked deleted and hidden
steps.detail: Deleted-at column set; share links stop working.

steps.text: After 30 days a job removes it from storage
steps.detail: Nightly purge job.

steps.text: At provider B, deleted files sit in a recycle area for 7 more days
steps.detail: Must be turned off, or counted inside our 30 days.

steps.text: During a move, the file may exist at both providers
steps.detail: Deletes must reach both until the old copy is gone.
steps.pain: A deleted file could survive at the old provider.

steps.text: Account closure deletes everything after 14 days
steps.detail: Same purge job, per account.

steps.text: We log that the file is gone
steps.detail: Logged for account closures only.

journeys.title: Moving existing files to provider B
journeys.summary: Copying 180 TB without customers noticing, if we decide to move.
creates: A copy of every file at provider B

steps.text: Ask provider B for free transfer in writing
steps.detail: 2 to 3 weeks for approval.

steps.text: Legal checks the new region against customer contracts
steps.detail: Different EU country from today.

steps.text: Create buckets at provider B with new names
steps.detail: Names are global; ours must change.

steps.text: Copy new uploads to both providers for a month
steps.detail: Dual writes from the upload service.

steps.text: Copy older files in batches overnight
steps.detail: Largest and most-downloaded first, to cut data out soonest.

steps.text: Compare checksums for every file
steps.detail: A report of any file that does not match.

steps.text: Switch reads to provider B, then writes
steps.detail: One setting per customer group, so we can switch back.

steps.text: Keep the old copy for 30 days, then delete it
steps.detail: Deletes made in those 30 days go to both.

journeys.title: When something goes wrong
journeys.summary: A storage outage, a stuck upload, or a missed completion message.

steps.text: Storage provider has an outage
steps.detail: Today uploads fail with a generic error.

steps.text: Customer sees a plain message and their upload pauses
steps.detail: Resume when storage is back, without starting over.

steps.text: A completion message never arrives
steps.detail: Nightly job finds files stuck in 'uploading' for over 24 hours.

steps.text: Stuck files are checked against storage and fixed or cleaned up
steps.detail: If the file is complete in storage, scan it; if not, delete the record.

steps.text: On-call is alerted when large-upload failures pass 2%
steps.detail: Today nobody is alerted; support finds out from tickets.

steps.text: Support can see a customer's recent uploads and why they failed
steps.detail: A simple page for support, read-only.

maps.title: Options
maps.intro: The outcome at the top, then the problems that stand in its way, the ideas for each, and the quick tests that would prove an idea.

root.title: Big uploads always finish, and the transfer bill falls

children.title: Ship to 5% of video uploads for two weeks
children.text: Compare failure rate and server load.

children.title: Raise the idle timeout to 10 minutes on one server
Copy one month of new files to B and serve them through the CDN
children.text: Measure the bill and download speed.

children.title: Cache popular downloads at the CDN
Turn on caching for public files only
children.text: One week, then compare data out.

gaps.title: Direct uploads with a progress bar and resume
gaps.why: Fixes the timeouts no matter which provider we use; uploads over 200 MB are 71% of all bytes.

stories.as: As a customer uploading a large video on a weak connection, I want the upload to resume where it stopped, so I do not start again.
done_when: a 2 GB upload survives a 30-second disconnect
the progress bar matches the bytes received
our servers handle no file bytes

stories.as: As a producer uploading a 4 GB video, I want to see how far along it is, so I know it is not stuck.
done_when: a progress bar shows percent and time left
it updates at least every 2 seconds

stories.as: As a school office behind a strict firewall, I want uploads to still work, so we are not locked out.
done_when: if the storage address cannot be reached within 5 seconds, the upload falls back to the old path
support can see which customers used the fallback

gaps.title: Scan files that never touch our servers
gaps.why: Today scanning assumes we saw the upload, and a bad file can be downloaded for up to 4 minutes.

stories.as: As the security engineer, I want every upload scanned before anyone can download it, so direct uploads add no risk.
done_when: a file is not downloadable until its scan passes
an infected test file is quarantined and the customer is told

stories.as: As a customer, I want to know my file is being checked, so a short wait makes sense.
done_when: the file shows 'Checking' until the scan passes
files under 100 MB are ready within 15 seconds

gaps.title: Move existing files to provider B
gaps.why: Cuts the data-out bill; only worth it if the free transfer is granted.

stories.as: As finance, I want the move to cost nothing up front, so the saving shows before the September review.
done_when: provider B confirms free transfer in writing
every file's checksum matches after the copy
downloads switch over with no broken links

stories.as: As the engineering lead, I want to switch back within an hour, so a bad move does not become an outage.
done_when: reads and writes switch by one setting per customer group
a dry run of switching back is done before the move

gaps.title: Serve popular files from the CDN
gaps.why: 18% of files cause 80% of data out; caching them cuts the bill with either provider.

stories.as: As finance, I want popular downloads to stop counting as data out, so the bill falls before September.
done_when: public and shared files are served from the CDN
data out falls at least 30% in the first month

stories.as: As a security engineer, I want private files never cached, so nobody gets someone else's file.
done_when: only files marked public or shared go to the CDN
a private file request always checks permission first

gaps.title: Deletes reach every copy
gaps.why: Our terms promise deleted files are gone within 30 days; provider B keeps a 7-day recycle area and a move means two copies.

stories.as: As a customer who deleted a file, I want it gone everywhere within 30 days, as the terms promise.
done_when: provider B's recycle area is off, or our purge runs 7 days early
deletes during the move go to both providers
a monthly check finds no deleted file older than 30 days

gaps.title: Know about failures before customers tell us
gaps.why: Support found out about the 2 May incident from 31 tickets.

stories.as: As on-call, I want an alert when large uploads start failing, so I can act in minutes, not hours.
done_when: an alert fires when failures over 200 MB pass 2% for 10 minutes
the alert links to a page showing the failing step

stories.as: As support, I want to see a customer's recent uploads and why they failed, so I can answer the ticket.
done_when: a read-only page lists the last 20 uploads with status and error
it never shows file contents

notes.title: The proxy is the bottleneck
notes.body: Servers hold a connection for the whole upload. That is why everything slowed down.
notes.recommend: Do direct uploads first; it is independent of the provider choice.
notes.question: Do we agree to separate the two decisions: direct uploads now, provider later?

notes.title: Signed links must be narrow
notes.body: A link that allows any path, or lasts hours, would let anyone write files into our storage.
notes.recommend: Links last 10 minutes, cover one path, and set a size limit.
notes.question: Is 10 minutes long enough for the slowest customers, given uploads resume in pieces?

notes.title: Nothing is downloadable before it is scanned
notes.body: With direct uploads, a file lands in storage before we have looked at it.
notes.recommend: Upload into a holding area; move it to the live area only after a clean scan.
notes.question: Who builds and tests the holding area before the 5% trial?

notes.title: Customers asked for two things
notes.body: A progress bar and resuming after a dropped connection. Neither needs a new provider.
notes.recommend: Ship both with direct uploads, and tell the 31 customers who raised tickets.
notes.question: Do we contact the customers who reported the problem when the fix ships?

notes.title: The bill problem is data out, not storage
notes.body: Storage grew a little; data out grew a lot.
notes.recommend: Try CDN caching first; it is cheap and fast to test.
notes.question: How much must data out fall by September for this to count as fixed?

notes.title: Only move if the transfer is free
notes.body: At $16,000, the move pays back in about seven months. Free transfer makes it pay back at once.
notes.recommend: Ask provider B for free transfer in writing before deciding.
notes.question: Who asks provider B, and by when?

notes.title: Two outcomes, two clocks
notes.body: Timeouts hurt customers now. The bill matters by September.
notes.recommend: Fix timeouts this month; decide the provider in July with test results in hand.
notes.question: Is July the right month to make the provider decision?

notes.title: Say what the trial must show
notes.body: Without a target, a two-week trial cannot pass or fail.
notes.recommend: Pass if failed uploads drop below 1% and no server spends more than 5% of its time on uploads.
notes.question: Are those the right pass marks for the trial?

notes.title: Tell people what is happening
notes.body: Today a big upload shows a spinner with no end.
notes.recommend: Show bytes sent, time left, and a clear message if the connection drops.
notes.question: Should a dropped upload resume by itself, or ask first?

notes.title: An assistant can check the copy
notes.body: Comparing checksums for millions of files is repetitive and easy to get wrong by hand.
notes.recommend: Let an agent run and report the checksum comparison; a person signs off the switch-over.
notes.question: Who signs off the switch-over once the agent's report is clean?

notes.title: Nobody has run provider B
notes.body: Four years of experience with the current provider; none with B.
notes.recommend: Run the one-month copy test before committing.
notes.question: Are we willing to run two providers for a few months during the move?

notes.title: Starting again from zero is the real pain
notes.body: The videographer lost two hours re-uploading the same file; four tickets came from hotel or train wifi.
notes.recommend: Make resume the first thing the trial measures.
notes.question: Do we promise resume in the help pages before the trial ends?

notes.title: Strict firewalls could lock some customers out
notes.body: A school office asked if the new way would work behind their firewall.
notes.recommend: Keep the old path as a fallback and tell support how to spot it.
notes.question: How long do we keep the old proxy path running as a fallback?

notes.title: Say plainly why a file was rejected
notes.body: Customers see 'Error' today, which looks like our fault.
notes.recommend: Show 'This file was blocked because it may contain a virus' and what to do next.
notes.question: Do we tell free-plan users the scanner's reason, or only that it was blocked?

notes.title: Show time left, not just percent
notes.body: A producer could not tell whether the upload was stuck.
notes.recommend: Show percent, speed and time left, updated every two seconds.
notes.question: Is time left accurate enough on weak connections to show it?

notes.title: One status field for every file
notes.body: Uploading, checking, ready and rejected must mean the same thing on every page.
notes.recommend: Write the four states down and use them in the app, support page and alerts.
notes.question: Do we need a separate state for files waiting on a fallback upload?

notes.title: Decide what counts as stuck
notes.body: Completion messages retry for 24 hours, so 'stuck' must be longer than that.
notes.recommend: Call a file stuck after 26 hours in 'uploading'.
notes.question: Is 26 hours too long for customers waiting on a file?

notes.title: We must answer completion messages quickly
notes.body: Provider B retries for 24 hours if we do not answer; slow answers cause duplicates.
notes.recommend: Answer at once and do the scan in a background job; ignore duplicates by upload id.
notes.question: Who owns the completion endpoint and its alerts?

notes.title: Dual writes double the risk of half-done uploads
notes.body: For a month every upload goes to two places.
notes.recommend: Treat the old provider as the source of truth until the switch; log every mismatch.
notes.question: Do we pause the move if mismatches pass 0.1%?

notes.title: No alert today
notes.body: Support found the incident from tickets; nobody was paged.
notes.recommend: Alert on large-upload failure rate, not on server errors alone.
notes.question: What failure rate should wake someone at night?

notes.title: Caching may beat moving
notes.body: Caching popular files cuts most data out without moving anything.
notes.recommend: Run the one-week caching test before deciding on provider B.
notes.question: If caching cuts data out by 30%, do we still move?

notes.title: Keep the fallback small
notes.body: A permanent second upload path doubles what we support.
notes.recommend: Keep the fallback for six months, then review who still uses it.
notes.question: Who reviews the fallback numbers in six months?

notes.title: The recycle area breaks our deletion promise
notes.body: Provider B keeps deleted files 7 days unless it is turned off; our terms promise 30 days in total.
notes.recommend: Turn the recycle area off, or purge 7 days early.
notes.question: Which do we choose: turn it off, or purge early?

notes.title: Never cache private files
notes.body: A cache mistake could show one customer's file to another.
notes.recommend: Cache only files marked public or shared; check permission for everything else.
notes.question: Who reviews the cache rules before the test?

notes.title: A new country needs a legal check
notes.body: Provider B's EU region is in a different country, and some contracts name the country.
notes.recommend: Ask legal for a list of affected customers before any copy starts.
notes.question: Do we need to tell customers before their files move country?

notes.title: An agent can clean up stuck uploads
notes.body: Checking each stuck record against storage is routine and rule-based.
notes.recommend: Let an agent fix or remove stuck records nightly and post a summary.
notes.question: Should the agent delete stuck records itself, or only list them for a person?

notes.title: An agent can draft the first support reply
notes.body: Most tickets ask the same three things.
notes.recommend: Draft a reply from the customer's upload history for support to check and send.
notes.question: Are we comfortable with an agent reading upload history to draft replies?

notes.title: Checksum reports are a good job for an agent
notes.body: Comparing 180 TB of checksums is long and repetitive.
notes.recommend: Let an agent run the comparison and flag only mismatches.
notes.question: Who acts on a mismatch: the agent, or a person?

notes.title: Every download costs money today
notes.body: $90 per TB of data out is most of the bill growth.
notes.recommend: Measure data out per customer plan so we know who drives it.
notes.question: Should heavy-download plans pay more?

notes.title: No written transfer, no move
notes.body: Moving 180 TB costs about $16,000 without the free transfer.
notes.recommend: Send the written request this week; it takes 2 to 3 weeks.
notes.question: Who sends the request, and do we wait for it before any other work?

notes.title: September is the deadline that matters
notes.body: Finance wants the bill down before the September review.
notes.recommend: Plan so that caching or the move shows in the August bill.
notes.question: Is the August bill the one we judge by?

notes.title: Measure the same thing before and after
notes.body: Failure rates differ a lot between busy hours and night.
notes.recommend: Report busy-hour and night rates separately.
notes.question: Do we judge the trial on busy-hour rates only?

notes.title: A short wait to download is fine if it is explained
notes.body: Customers accept 'Checking' if they can see it.
notes.recommend: Show 'Checking for viruses, usually under 15 seconds'.
notes.question: Do we let the uploader download their own file before the scan?

decisions.question: Do we build direct uploads now, separately from the provider choice?
decisions.decision: Yes. Direct uploads ship to 5% of video uploads in June.

decisions.question: Do we move to provider B?
How do signed links and scanning work?
Do we run the one-week caching test before deciding on provider B?
How do we keep the 30-day deletion promise at provider B?

outcomes.measure: Time from upload to 'Ready' for files under 100 MB
